one_liner: LLVM-based ahead-of-time compiler for a statically typed Python subset; 10-90x faster than CPython, mostly ahead of PyPy.
what_it_does: Codon compiles Python-syntax programs end to end into native executables (`codon build -release`), or runs them with `codon run`. It can also build Python extension modules or JIT individual functions from CPython via the `codon-jit` pip package and its @codon.jit decorator. It is not a CPython drop-in: types are inferred statically, collections must be homogeneous, `int` is a 64-bit machine integer, and modules without a Codon-native implementation are reached through a CPython bridge (`from python import ...`, with CODON_PYTHON pointing at libpython).
how_it_is_fast: Whole-program static type inference turns Python code into monomorphic, unboxed code. Tuples compile to structs and library code is inlined with no object files, and the result is optimized by an LLVM 20-based fork. Codon adds its own IR passes for Python-level patterns (for example fusion in its native NumPy) and has no interpreter or VM at run time; memory is managed by the Boehm conservative garbage collector. Native threads without a GIL (@par over OpenMP) and GPU kernels give further speedups beyond the single-thread numbers.
when_to_use: CPU-bound pure-Python kernels (loops over ints and floats, small-object trees, string scanning, interpreters) that you can compile as a standalone program or extension: 2-90x over CPython 3.10.7 in the independent suite
Code where PyPy is the current speedup: Codon beat PyPy 7.3.11 on 8 of 10 kernels that ran (brainfuck2 1.91 s vs 11.03 s, nbody 2.23 s vs 4.44 s, binarytrees 1.0 s vs 3.84 s)
Batch or HPC jobs that can use @par multithreading or GPU kernels, which CPython's GIL rules out
Hot functions inside a larger CPython codebase via @codon.jit or the extension build mode, when the function uses statically typeable Python
when_not_to_use: Programs that need arbitrary-precision ints, heterogeneous containers, runtime monkey patching or other dynamic features: int is 64-bit by default and these are rejected at compile time (pidigits, regexdna and revcomp failed to run in the independent suite)
Workloads dominated by C-implemented libraries, I/O or the network; the FAQ says these see no substantial speedup
Allocation-heavy code that creates many short-lived objects: issue #553 (open) reports a ray tracer twice as slow as PyPy with more than half the time in the Boehm GC's alloc_atomic
fannkuchredux- and mandelbrot-style kernels, where PyPy was faster (0.71 s vs 1.82 s, 0.54 s vs 0.65 s)
Short scripts where the 4-6 s compile time per program outweighs the run time, and Windows without WSL

integration.form: compiler toolchain (CLI producing native executables, shared libraries or Python extension modules) plus the codon-jit pip package
integration.dependencies: prebuilt install via exaloop's install.sh; building from source needs Codon's LLVM fork (based on LLVM 20, with openmp and compiler-rt) and libgfortran; Boehm GC is bundled; Python interop needs a CPython shared library set via CODON_PYTHON
integration.min_toolchain: Codon CLI 0.20.x current (benchmarked 0.15.5); source build needs CMake, Clang and Python 3.8+ for the build step
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS natively (docs timings on an M1, independent suite on x86-64); Windows only through WSL
integration.thread_safety: No GIL; @par loops run on OpenMP threads, and simple reductions such as `total += 1` become atomic automatically. Thread safety of built-in containers under concurrent mutation is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — much Python source compiles unchanged, but it is not a CPython replacement: 64-bit ints, static typing, compile-time-sized tuples, C numeric semantics unless -numerics=py, and CPython modules only through the bridge

gotchas: The independent numbers come from Codon 0.15.5, which used ASCII strings and unordered dicts. Since v0.20, Unicode strings and insertion-ordered dicts are the defaults, and the docs say the old unordered dict (`-unordered-dict`) 'generally performs better', so the string- and dict-heavy rows (knucleotide, fasta, brainfuck) may not reproduce on current Codon defaults.

Codon ran adapted test.codon.py sources; most changes are cosmetic (f-strings, typed class fields, a typed Dict), but CPython and PyPy ran matmul over array.array('d') rows, which box a new float on every read, while Codon used plain lists. That skews the CPython matmul ratio (22.73 s vs 0.25 s) somewhat in Codon's favour. Codon's nbody uses copy.copy instead of copy.deepcopy, so in-process repetitions 2-5 start from the mutated state of run 1. The operation count is unchanged and the correctness check runs only once, so timing is not materially affected.

Integer overflow follows 64-bit machine semantics, and division by zero and math-domain checks follow C semantics unless -numerics=py is passed; results can differ silently from CPython on large integers.

The best-time column excludes Codon's 4.3-6.4 s compile time, and several PyPy and knucleotide rows are single runs; `codon run` without -release is unoptimized (fib(40): 0.43 s vs 0.31 s with -release in the docs).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Codon over PyPy when the program fits the static subset and runs long enough to amortize the compile, since it led PyPy on 8 of 10 kernels and adds GIL-free threads; pick PyPy for unmodified dynamic Python, bigints or fannkuch-like code. Over Cython and mypyc, Codon needs no .pyx or C-API knowledge and was far faster on interpreter-style code (brainfuck 2.05 s vs Cython 165.97 s and mypyc 93.55 s), though Cython won binarytrees (0.81 s vs 1.0 s) and fannkuchredux (0.13 s vs 1.82 s) in the same suite.
verified_claims_summary: On kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10, best in-program time with compile time excluded), Codon 0.15.5 binaries built with `codon build --release` beat CPython 3.10.7 by about 2x to 90x (fannkuchredux 1.82 s vs 4.04 s, binarytrees 1.0 s vs 73.15 s). They beat PyPy 7.3.11 on 8 of 10 kernels (brainfuck 2.05 s vs 8.77 s, matmul 0.25 s vs 0.36 s), lost on fannkuchredux and mandelbrot, and failed pidigits, regexdna and revcomp. The suite's check step compares small-input output with expected text, and Codon is on no expected-failure list.
status_note: Actively maintained by Exaloop (v0.20.3 on 2026-09-28, 16.9k stars, 95 open issues) and Apache-2.0 since v0.18; the benchmarked 0.15.5 was under BSL-1.1, so use a v0.18+ release for unrestricted use.
